principle_text: When the seller offers a discounted price and the buyer accepts without further negotiation, express gratitude to confirm agreement and secure a favorable outcome.
When the buyer addresses the seller's stated reason for the high price by offering assistance, the buyer should leverage this by proposing a reduced price, enhancing negotiation outcomes.
When the seller expresses emotional attachment to the item but mentions financial need, you should leverage the seller's emotional connection to negotiate a lower price effectively.

When the seller offers additional items and raises the price, avoid conceding too quickly by increasing your offer, as it may weaken your negotiating position and shift the focus away from securing a lower price.
When the seller offers a reduced price and additional items, avoid accepting the offer without negotiating for further concessions to improve your position in the negotiation.
When the seller offers additional items and a discounted price, you should express agreement to signal mutual acceptance and finalize a deal at a more favorable price point.

When the buyer offers a specific price below the seller's initial demand, proposes immediate pickup, and acknowledges the item's condition, the seller should consider accepting the offer to move the negotiation towards a lower price.
When the seller has agreed to a price lower than their initial asking price, avoid simply acknowledging their acceptance without further negotiation or clarification.
When the seller mentions another interested buyer willing to pay more, avoid conceding ground by offering a price significantly higher than your target, weakening your negotiation leverage.

When the seller is faced with a buyer offering a lower price but emphasizing immediate pickup to accommodate the seller's convenience, the seller should consider accepting the revised offer to secure a timely sale.
When the seller has already accepted the buyer's offer, avoid reconfirming the agreed-upon price as it does not contribute to further negotiation progress.
When the seller is willing to negotiate a fair price but nothing too crazy, you should anchor the negotiation by making a specific low offer to push the seller towards a more favorable price.

When the seller is motivated to get rid of the item, offering a compromise between the buyer's and seller's proposed prices, along with additional convenience benefits, can lead to a successful negotiation.

When the seller emphasizes the antique value and great condition of the item, avoid asking questions that inadvertently strengthen the seller's position without challenging the price or proposing a counteroffer.
When the seller admits to visible scratches on the item but presents an easy fix, you should leverage this information to negotiate a lower price based on the need for repair work.
When the seller confirms visible scratches on the item, you should leverage this flaw to negotiate a lower price effectively.
When the seller has already made a counteroffer, avoid accepting it without attempting to negotiate further to secure a better deal.
When the seller has already reduced the price once, you should emphasize urgency and budget constraints to strengthen your leverage and move the price closer to your target.
When the buyer shows immediate agreement to the seller's counteroffer without further negotiation, it concedes ground and weakens the bargaining position, potentially leading to a higher final price.
When the seller offers a lower price than their initial asking price, avoid accepting the offer too quickly without further negotiation to potentially secure a more favorable deal.
When the buyer asks about details already stated in the item description, avoid repeating information to prevent wasting negotiation time and focus on price and terms instead.
When the seller offers a bundled discount to close the deal, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to potentially secure a better price.
When the seller offers a price reduction contingent on the buyer assuming a cost or effort, you should confirm acceptance clearly to secure the favorable terms efficiently.
When the seller proposes a counteroffer closer to their desired price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller has already accepted your price offer and asks for a preference detail, avoid making further price demands that do not relate to the agreed terms.
When the seller responds to a low offer with a counteroffer above the buyer's maximum, you should make a small concession to encourage the seller to lower their price closer to your target.
When the seller offers a conditional price reduction to encourage quick purchase, avoid immediately agreeing without attempting to negotiate further or propose a counteroffer.
When the seller makes a conditional lower price offer including extras, avoid conceding too quickly on price without leveraging terms to maintain negotiation strength.
When the seller makes a clear and reasonable counteroffer close to your target price, you should accept it promptly to secure a favorable deal without unnecessary further negotiation.
When the seller clearly states their initial price and item condition, avoid passive acknowledgments that do not challenge or counteroffer, as they fail to create negotiation leverage.
When the seller expresses concern about logistical challenges like delivery, you should offer immediate payment and pickup to increase your leverage and encourage price flexibility.
When the seller states a firm minimum price, avoid immediately accepting that price without attempting to negotiate further or explore alternative terms to maintain leverage.
When the seller has made a reasonable counteroffer, you should present a firm budget constraint and offer to reduce the seller's effort or costs to encourage acceptance of a lower price.
When the seller offers a price reduction contingent on a specific buyer action, you should confirm your willingness to fulfill that condition to secure the agreed-upon lower price.
When the seller sets a firm counteroffer with specific conditions, avoid immediately accepting the higher price without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage.
When the seller counters with a price close to their original asking point after your offer, avoid making concessions that narrow the price gap without gaining additional leverage or benefits.
When the seller makes a firm counteroffer close to their asking price, avoid immediately accepting a price above your stated maximum limit to maintain negotiation leverage.
When the seller firmly states a price and highlights the item’s value, avoid increasing your offer too quickly as it reduces your leverage in price negotiations.
When the seller clearly states a firm minimum price and rejects a very low offer, avoid making an initial offer that is too far below their stated minimum as it may stall negotiation progress.

When the seller shows urgency to sell quickly and values convenience, you should offer a reasonable price reduction combined with terms that reduce the seller's effort or costs to increase acceptance likelihood.

When the seller sets a minimum price based on delivery convenience, you should propose a slightly lower price combined with self-pickup to reduce the seller's costs and improve your bargaining position.
When the seller responds to a direct price reduction request by agreeing but adding conditions, avoid immediately increasing your offer as it weakens your negotiating leverage.
When the seller agrees to a conditional price reduction, avoid shifting focus to unrelated product details that do not further negotiate the price or terms.
When the seller responds to a buyer's increased offer by raising their counteroffer, avoid conceding ground too quickly without securing a better deal.
When the seller has already accepted your price offer, avoid making additional remarks that do not advance the negotiation or clarify terms.

When the seller offers a price contingent on buyer pickup and cannot provide delivery, avoid requesting delivery at that price as it introduces logistical constraints that do not improve negotiation leverage.
When the seller confirms the item is sturdy with minor cosmetic blemishes, avoid asking only neutral questions that do not leverage this information to negotiate a better price.
When the seller introduces a logistical condition like pickup, avoid agreeing to it without first negotiating a price concession to maintain leverage in the price negotiation.
When the seller offers a counterprice with added services, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.

When the seller firmly states a minimum acceptable price and rejects low offers, avoid making small incremental concessions that do not approach the seller’s minimum, as this weakens your negotiation leverage.

When the seller firmly states a minimum acceptable price but shows concern about loss, you should introduce conditional offers involving additional perks to create negotiation flexibility beyond just price.
When the seller indicates a firm minimum price but is open to non-monetary concessions, avoid asking open-ended questions that shift focus away from negotiating a lower price.

When the seller indicates a firm minimum price above your initial offers, avoid immediately accepting their counteroffer without attempting to negotiate additional concessions or reaffirm your lower limit.
When the seller expresses reluctance but shows openness to negotiation, you should introduce a conditional offer that benefits the seller to encourage price concessions.
When the seller emphasizes the item's condition without adjusting the price, avoid focusing on unrelated product details that do not directly support negotiating a lower price.
When the seller states their lowest acceptable price, you should make a firm, clear counteroffer that respects this limit while adding value through alternative payment options.
When the seller sets a firm lowest acceptable price and requests cash, you should enhance your offer with additional non-cash value to increase appeal without lowering your cash payment.
When the seller maintains a firm price above your initial offer, you should assertively restate your target price to encourage the seller to lower their counteroffer closer to your desired amount.
When the seller counters with a price moderately above your initial offer and adds value extras, you should propose a reasonable middle-ground offer to encourage acceptance and secure a better deal.
When the seller describes minor flaws and sets a firm price, you should make a lower counteroffer while referencing those flaws to justify your offer and encourage acceptance.
When the seller has agreed to a reasonable price and confirmed the buyer's offer, avoid making neutral acknowledgments that do not further negotiate or clarify terms.
When the seller links a price reduction to a specific buyer action, you should agree to that action to demonstrate willingness and move the negotiation toward closing the deal.

When the seller sets a firm minimum price but responds to a higher buyer offer with additional non-price demands, avoid accepting conditional offers that complicate the negotiation and increase your total cost.
When the seller adds a non-monetary condition to a price offer that the buyer cannot accept, you should propose a slightly higher price to remove the condition while still securing a favorable deal.
When the seller has already accepted a final price offer, avoid making neutral acknowledgments that do not seek to improve or clarify the agreement terms.
When the seller sets a firm but negotiable price and requests immediate pickup, you should offer prompt payment and convenience incentives to encourage a further price reduction.
When the seller clearly states their lowest acceptable price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting to negotiate further or explore alternative concessions.
When the seller states their firm asking price, you should respond with a clear counteroffer that reflects your target price to establish your negotiation position early.
When the seller maintains a firm price including delivery, you should leverage pickup options to justify a lower offer and encourage a price reduction.
When the seller has just agreed to a lower price, you should leverage that agreement to request additional value, such as including extra items, to improve the overall deal without raising the price.
When the seller makes a counteroffer that includes additional value like delivery, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to improve the price.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate but holds firm on price, you should offer a slightly higher cash amount combined with a small non-monetary incentive to encourage immediate acceptance.
When the seller states a firm price but hints at flexibility, you should propose a specific lower offer with a condition to encourage a seller concession.
When the seller states a firm price but is open to negotiation, avoid accepting the initial price without attempting to negotiate a lower price or better terms.
When the seller states a firm price per item but has multiple units available, you should propose a bulk purchase at your target price to encourage immediate agreement.
When the seller firmly maintains a high price by emphasizing the item's value and original cost, avoid increasing your offer combined with non-monetary favors that reduce your leverage.
When the seller emphasizes the item's good condition and justifies a high price, you should directly ask for their lowest acceptable price to clarify negotiation boundaries and gain leverage.

When the seller maintains a firm price above your offer, avoid increasing your bid too quickly as it may encourage the seller to raise their counteroffer instead of moving closer to your target price.
When the seller counters with a price close to your offer, you should agree to the price while negotiating additional terms that add value, such as delivery, to improve the overall deal.
When the seller firmly states a price and delivery terms, you should make a clear, reasonable counteroffer that improves your position while maintaining key conditions.
When the seller agrees to a price reduction contingent on immediate pickup, avoid simply confirming logistics without attempting to negotiate further price improvements.
When the seller invites your budget range to explore flexibility, you should present a firm, low initial offer to create leverage and encourage a significant price concession.
When the seller makes a clear counteroffer with added value, avoid immediately accepting without attempting to negotiate further for a better price or additional benefits.
When the seller adds non-essential incentives to justify a higher price, you should reject those extras and firmly restate your offer to focus the negotiation on the core item's value.
When the seller acknowledges your price concerns but offers a counter higher than your initial offer, avoid lowering your offer further as it can weaken your negotiation leverage.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer that reduces the price significantly, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to preserve leverage for a better deal.
When the seller highlights product features and added services without changing the price, avoid shifting focus away from negotiating price concessions too early.
When the seller offers additional value like delivery and setup, you should present a specific lower counteroffer tied to your financial constraints to encourage a downward price adjustment.
When the seller firmly maintains their initial price without concession, avoid making aggressive low offers that undermine your own leverage and reduce negotiation flexibility.
When the seller holds firm on price and offers a concession on service, avoid conceding on price too quickly without securing a counteroffer or agreement.
When the seller shows reluctance to lower a fair price but indicates urgency to sell, you should propose a justified lower offer to leverage their need and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller has stated a firm price including delivery and seeks confirmation, avoid simply accepting without attempting to negotiate further or explore additional terms.
When the seller has clearly stated their minimum acceptable price and delivery terms, avoid immediately accepting without attempting to negotiate for a better deal or additional concessions.
When the seller has accepted your price and added a bonus item, avoid repeating acceptance without introducing new negotiation points or requests.
